section.title: Do Not Fret Because of the Wicked
section.sectionRationale: A wisdom acrostic psalm, each strophe once paired to a letter of the Hebrew alphabet, wrestling with the perennial problem of the wicked's brief flourishing. It closes Book I, Psalms 1-41, returning to that book's opening contrast between the righteous and the wicked, but now from the vantage point of a long life, 'I once was young and now am old', verse 25.
section.thesis: David counsels against fretting or envying the wicked's fleeting prosperity, calling the righteous instead to trust, delight in, and wait for the LORD, who sees, judges justly, and will give the meek the land, a hope Jesus takes up directly when He blesses the meek with the inheritance of the earth.
section.frameNote: Eight movements following the acrostic's turning wheel: the call not to fret but trust, verses 1-6; be still and wait, verses 7-11; the wicked's schemes and their certain end, verses 12-17; the LORD's care for the blameless, verses 18-22; a lifetime's testimony that the righteous are not forsaken, verses 23-26; turning from evil to keep God's way, verses 27-31; the wicked lying in wait yet not prevailing, verses 32-36; and the closing contrast of the future of the wicked and the salvation of the righteous, verses 37-40.

units.label: Do not fret, but trust and delight in the Lord

verses.text: Do not fret over those who do evil; do not envy those who do wrong.
For they wither quickly like grass and wilt like tender plants.
Trust in the LORD and do good; dwell in the land and cultivate faithfulness.
Delight yourself in the LORD, and He will give you the desires of your heart.
Commit your way to the LORD; trust in Him, and He will do it.
He will bring forth your righteousness like the dawn, your justice like the noonday sun.

units.label: Be still and wait patiently
units.note: the meek will inherit the land

verses.text: Be still before the LORD and wait patiently for Him; do not fret when men prosper in their ways, when they carry out wicked schemes.
Refrain from anger and abandon wrath; do not fret, it can only bring harm.
For the evildoers will be cut off, but those who {{qavah|hope}} in the LORD will inherit the land.
Yet a little while, and the wicked will be no more; though you look for them, they will not be found.
But the {{anavim|meek}} will inherit the land and delight in abundant prosperity.

units.label: The wicked scheme, but the Lord upholds the righteous
units.note: swords that pierce their own hearts

verses.text: The wicked scheme against the righteous and gnash their teeth at them,
but the Lord laughs, seeing that their day is coming.
The wicked have drawn the sword and bent the bow to bring down the poor and needy, to slay those whose ways are upright.
But their swords will pierce their own hearts, and their bows will be broken.
Better is the little of the righteous than the abundance of many who are wicked.
For the arms of the wicked will be broken, but the LORD upholds the righteous.

units.label: The Lord knows the days of the blameless

verses.text: The LORD knows the days of the blameless, and their inheritance will last forever.
In the time of evil they will not be ashamed, and in the days of famine they will be satisfied.
But the wicked and enemies of the LORD will perish like the glory of the fields. They will vanish; like smoke they will fade away.
The wicked borrow and do not repay, but the righteous are gracious and giving.
Surely those He blesses will inherit the land, but the cursed will be destroyed.

units.label: A lifetime's testimony
units.note: never have I seen the righteous abandoned

verses.text: The steps of a man are ordered by the LORD who takes delight in his journey.
Though he falls, he will not be overwhelmed, for the LORD is holding his hand.

I once was young and now am old, yet never have I seen the righteous abandoned 
or their children begging for bread.
They are ever generous and quick to lend, and their children are a blessing.

units.label: Turn from evil and do good
units.note: the law of God in the heart

verses.text: Turn away from evil and do good, so that you will abide forever.
For the LORD loves justice and will not forsake His {{chasidim|saints}}. They are preserved forever, but the offspring of the wicked will be cut off.
The righteous will inherit the land and dwell in it forever.
The mouth of the righteous man utters wisdom, and his tongue speaks justice.
The law of his God is in his heart; his steps do not falter.

units.label: The wicked lie in wait, yet do not prevail

verses.text: Though the wicked lie in wait for the righteous, and seek to slay them,
the LORD will not leave them in their power or let them be condemned under judgment.
{{qavah|Wait}} for the LORD and keep His way, and He will raise you up to inherit the land. When the wicked are cut off, you will see it.
I have seen a wicked, ruthless man flourishing like a well-rooted native tree,
yet he passed away and was no more; though I searched, he could not be found.

units.label: The future of the wicked and the salvation of the righteous

verses.text: Consider the blameless and observe the upright, for posterity awaits the man of peace.
But the transgressors will all be destroyed; the future of the wicked will be cut off.
The salvation of the righteous is from the LORD; He is their stronghold in time of trouble.

The LORD helps and delivers them; He rescues and saves them from the wicked, 
because they take refuge in Him.

qavah.gloss: To wait with expectant hope, from a root meaning to stretch or tense like a cord, picturing eager, taut waiting rather than passive resignation. The righteous hope in the LORD, verse 9, and are commanded to wait for Him, verse 34.

anavim.gloss: The meek, humble, or afflicted, those who have learned dependence on God rather than self-assertion. Jesus takes up this exact promise in Matthew 5:5, 'Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth.'

chasidim.gloss: His saints or godly ones, from chesed, God's covenant loving devotion. Those bound to God in loyal love are themselves shaped by that love and will not be forsaken.

basic.context: Written from the vantage point of a long life, verse 25, this wisdom psalm answers a problem every generation faces: the wicked often seem to prosper while the righteous struggle. David's counsel is not to fret or envy but to trust, delight in, commit to, and wait for the LORD, confident that the wicked's flourishing is as brief as grass and that the meek will inherit the land.
basic.hermeneutics: This is wisdom literature, not a blanket promise of material prosperity to every righteous person in every circumstance. It calls for a settled trust that outlasts appearances, grounded in the LORD's justice being sure even when it is not yet visible.
basic.originalLanguages: The psalm repeatedly uses qavah, to wait with taut, expectant hope, and commends the anavim, the meek or humble, who will inherit the land, the exact promise Jesus repeats in Matthew 5:5. It also calls the righteous chasidim, those shaped by God's chesed, His covenant loving devotion.
basic.typology: The land-inheritance promised to the meek and the righteous anticipates the wider, truer inheritance the New Testament describes, Abraham and his offspring inheriting the world, Romans 4:13, and finally the meek inheriting the earth in the kingdom Jesus proclaims, Matthew 5:5.
basic.christ: Jesus takes up this psalm's central promise word for word, 'Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth,' Matthew 5:5, reshaping Israel's land promise into the kingdom's full and final inheritance. He also lived the psalm's pattern perfectly, committing His way entirely to the Father, entrusting Himself to Him who judges justly even while suffering unjustly, 1 Peter 2:23.
basic.god: God is shown seeing every scheme of the wicked and laughing, not with cruelty but with the calm certainty of one who already knows how it ends, while at the same time ordering the steps of the righteous, delighting in their way, and holding their hand so that a fall never becomes a final ruin.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 5:5 takes up the promise that the meek will inherit the land, now the whole earth. Proverbs 3:5-6 echoes the call to trust the LORD rather than lean on one's own understanding. 1 Peter 2:23 shows Christ Himself entrusting His cause to God who judges justly, the pattern this psalm commends.
basic.oneStory: The wicked's flourishing is brief as grass, but the LORD upholds, sustains, and finally saves the righteous who trust, wait, and delight in Him, a hope brought to its fullest expression in Jesus, who blesses the meek with the inheritance of the earth and who Himself trusted the Father completely through suffering to glory.

context.literary:
Psalm 37 is an alphabetic acrostic, each new letter opening a fresh stanza, and unlike the shorter acrostics it lets each letter run for two verses or more, so that its lines behave less like proverbs than like short sermons. The alphabet gives the poem its slow, steady pace. Nothing in it hurries, and that is the point of a psalm about waiting.

The poem is held together by a small set of repeated phrases. Three times the opening command returns, 'do not fret', verses 1, 7 and 8, and the third time the reason is blunt: it 'can only bring harm'. The promise that the righteous 'will inherit the land' sounds like a refrain, at verses 9, 11, 22, 29 and 34. The threat that the wicked 'will be cut off' answers it at verses 9, 22, 28, 34 and 38. Because the two refrains fall together, in verses 9, 22 and 34, the poem keeps setting inheritance and excision side by side, as the two futures between which every hearer stands.

The commands come in clusters. Verses 3 to 5 stack four in a row, trust, delight, commit, trust, and verses 7 and 8 add be still, wait, refrain and abandon. Later come turn away from evil and do good, verse 27, wait and keep His way, verse 34, and consider and observe, verse 37. The psalm therefore teaches by a dense series of postures the whole person is to adopt, from the mind to the will to the body.

Two moments of personal testimony frame the second half and mirror each other. In verse 25 David says he has never seen the righteous abandoned or their children begging bread. In verses 35 and 36 he says he saw a wicked man flourishing like a well-rooted tree, and then 'he passed away and was no more; though I searched, he could not be found'. One observation is about what did not happen to the righteous, the other about what did happen to the wicked. Both are offered as evidence.

Some phrases also link the psalm to its neighbours. 'Turn away from evil and do good', verse 27, is the same instruction as Psalm 34:14, and the word for 'the meek', anavim, in verse 11 is the word used of the oppressed who hear and rejoice in Psalm 34:2.
context.historical:
The superscription reads only 'Of David', and verse 25, 'I once was young and now am old', suggests the poem comes from his later life. That fits the wisdom form, since it is the voice of an old man who has watched many careers rise and fall. It also fits a king who had seen the two extremes: he had known the prosperity of Saul's court, and the misery of being hunted by it.

The problem the psalm addresses was as old as Israel's faith. Job asks, 'Why do the wicked live on, growing old and increasing in power?', Job 21:7, Jeremiah says, 'Why does the way of the wicked prosper?', Jeremiah 12:1, and Malachi's contemporaries complain, 'Not only do evildoers prosper, they even test God and escape', Malachi 3:15. Psalm 73 is the closest parallel, with the confession, 'I envied the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked', Psalm 73:3, resolved only when 'I entered God's sanctuary; then I discerned their end', Psalm 73:17. Psalm 37 answers the same question from a different angle, by long observation and by waiting.

The promise of 'the land' is the most concrete feature of the psalm. Israel's whole life turned on the gift of the land that God 'swore He would give to your fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob', Deuteronomy 1:8. In an agricultural society the land was the family's inheritance, its food and its future, and to be cut off from it was the worst curse, Deuteronomy 28:63. The psalm's practical details belong to the same world: grass that withers in the heat, the borrower who does not repay, verse 21, the generous person who lends freely, verse 26, in obedience to the law that told Israelites to 'open your hand' to the poor, Deuteronomy 15:7-8, and the children who do not have to beg for bread, verse 25.

The image of the bow and the sword, verses 14 and 15, reflects a society in which the powerful could simply attack the poor. The psalm would have been sung in gatherings of people who were vulnerable to that, and it told them that patience was not weakness.
context.canonical:
Psalm 37 continues the argument that Psalm 1 opened the Psalter with: two ways, the righteous like a tree and the wicked like chaff, Psalm 1:3-4. In Psalm 37 the wicked are grass that withers and smoke that vanishes, verses 2 and 20. It also picks up the laughter of Psalm 2:4, 'The One enthroned in heaven laughs', in verse 13, and the promise of Psalm 25:13, that the faithful man's 'descendants will inherit the land'. The proverbs treat the same problem in almost the same words: 'Do not fret over evildoers, and do not be envious of the wicked', Proverbs 24:19, and 'surely there is a future, and your hope will not be cut off', Proverbs 23:18.

The New Testament takes up the psalm directly, and in a surprising way. Jesus says, 'Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth', Matthew 5:5, and the Bible's own footnote at Psalm 37:11 notes that the Hebrew can mean 'the earth' as well as 'the land'. Jesus takes the promise made to the meek in Israel and reads it at its widest. Paul extends it further: the promise to Abraham 'that he would be heir of the world', Romans 4:13. Hebrews sees Abraham and the patriarchs as people who lived as strangers in the promised land, 'longing for a better country', Hebrews 11:9 and 11:13-16. And in Revelation the promise is fulfilled: 'The one who overcomes will inherit all things', Revelation 21:7.

The call to patient waiting is echoed by James, who says, 'Be patient, then, brothers, until the Lord's coming', James 5:7-8, and by Peter, who points to Christ, who 'entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly', 1 Peter 2:23. The psalm's answer to the problem of the wicked is therefore not overturned but carried forward, and in the New Testament it is Christ's own example.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
David wrote to calm an anxiety that many believers know. When the wicked do well, the heart heats up. It burns with envy, with anger, and with the suspicion that faithfulness is a waste. The psalm opens with three warnings against this fever, and its whole purpose is to give the hearer something better to do with his heart.

What he gives is a set of postures. Trust, delight, commit and wait describe a life turned toward the LORD and away from the fret. He wants his hearers to see that these are not passive. 'Do good', 'dwell in the land', and 'cultivate faithfulness', verse 3, all describe ordinary, active obedience, and the psalm treats the daily practice of righteousness as part of the trust. The commands to be generous, verses 21 and 26, show that he expected patience to look like open hands and not clenched fists.

He also wanted his hearers to take the long view. 'Yet a little while', verse 10, sets the wicked man's success against the whole of a life and a whole of history. David's testimony is that of a man who has watched both, and the point of his observations is that the story is not over. His hearers were meant to understand that faithfulness is not measured by the short-term score, and that the LORD is a keeper of promises who will give the inheritance to those who wait.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm is wisdom, and wisdom speaks in generalisations that are true in the main. It does not say that every righteous person will always be comfortable, and the psalm itself knows this: it speaks of famine, verse 19, of the poor and needy attacked by the wicked, verse 14, of times of trouble, verse 39, and of a person who falls, verse 24. Verse 25 is one man's observation across a long life, and it should be read as such, and not as a legal guarantee.

The promise in verse 4, 'He will give you the desires of your heart', needs the same care. It sits after the command to delight in the LORD, and the whole psalm shapes what those desires will be. It is a description of how God deals with those whose deepest delight is in Him, not a formula for getting whatever one wants. If it is read as a promise of prosperity to anyone who uses the right technique, it turns the psalm upside down, since delight in the LORD is the reward and not the price.

What carries forward as command is clear. Do not fret, do not envy, trust, delight, commit, be still, wait, refrain from anger, turn from evil and do good. These are as binding now as when David wrote them. The land promise carries forward as a promise, but in the way the New Testament reads it: the meek inherit the earth, Matthew 5:5, in the renewed creation that Christ shares with His people, and the wicked's short flourishing is not the end of the story.

debates.question: What is the 'land' that the meek and the righteous will inherit?

views.label: The land of Israel
views.case: The Hebrew word is the ordinary word for 'the land', and the promise is set in the frame of the covenant with Abraham, whose descendants were to possess Canaan, Deuteronomy 1:8. On this view David is promising his hearers that those who stay faithful will keep their land and homes, while the wicked will be uprooted.

views.label: Heaven, or the spiritual blessings of the covenant
views.case: Some early and later Christian readers took 'the land' as a picture of the heavenly country, as Hebrews 11:13-16 does for Abraham. On this reading the promise is spiritual and eternal, and it explains why some righteous people in this life lose everything.

views.label: The renewed earth, in Christ
views.case: Jesus reads the promise as 'the earth', Matthew 5:5, and Paul says Abraham was to be 'heir of the world', Romans 4:13. On this view the land promise was always a down payment on the restored creation, and it is inherited through Christ, the heir of all things, Hebrews 1:2, in the new earth where righteousness dwells, 2 Peter 3:13.

debates.bearing: The third view fits best with how the New Testament actually quotes the psalm. It does not remove the first meaning, since God did give Israel a land and the promise was real, but it shows the land was a pointer to something wider. Reading the promise as escape to another world misses the biblical hope of the renewed earth.

debates.question: How should we read 'never have I seen the righteous abandoned' in verse 25?

views.label: A personal observation, proverbially true
views.case: David says what he has seen, and wisdom literature often speaks in general patterns. On this reading the verse describes the ordinary course of God's care in the covenant community, where the righteous were supported by their neighbours in obedience to the law, Deuteronomy 15:7-8, and it does not deny exceptions.

views.label: True in the end, not always in the moment
views.case: The righteous can suffer want for a time, and Jesus tells of a poor man, Lazarus, who lay at a rich man's gate, longing for crumbs, Luke 16:20-21. Hebrews speaks of believers who were 'destitute, oppressed, and mistreated', of whom 'the world was not worthy', Hebrews 11:37-38. On this view the verse is true only when the whole story is told, including what comes after death.

views.label: Ultimately true because One was forsaken
views.case: There is one righteous man who cried, 'My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?', Psalm 22:1 and Matthew 27:46. The word for 'abandoned' in verse 25 is the root of that word. On this reading, the promise that the righteous are not finally abandoned is secured by the One who was, and 'God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf', 2 Corinthians 5:21.

debates.bearing: These readings work together more than they compete. The verse is a true observation of God's usual care, it needs the horizon of eternity to be fully true of every believer, and the cross is the reason it can be spoken with confidence. It is not safe to use it as a simple promise of comfort without all three.

study.originalLanguages:
The psalm's first command, 'do not fret', uses a verb that literally means to burn or grow hot, and the same word describes Cain's rage when his offering was refused, 'Cain became very angry', Genesis 4:5. It occurs three times, verses 1, 7 and 8, and in the third the psalm adds that anger and fretting lead only to harm. The picture is of a heart that overheats while watching others succeed, and the cure is a cooler word, 'Be still before the LORD', verse 7. That verb is dom, to be silent or hushed, and it is the same root as the 'be still' of Psalm 4:4.

Verse 4 says, 'Delight yourself in the LORD, and He will give you the desires of your heart.' The verb for delight, hith'anag, is the reflexive form of a word for pleasure, and it is used in Isaiah 58:14, 'then you will delight yourself in the LORD'. The word for 'desires' is not the usual word for wanting. It comes from the verb to ask, and it is the word behind 'petitions' in Psalm 20:5, 'May the LORD grant all your petitions'. What is promised is the granting of requests, and the psalm has just described a person whose requests are shaped by delighting in God. The same verb of delight returns in verse 11, where the meek 'delight in abundant prosperity', literally in an abundance of shalom, peace, so that the delight in the LORD in verse 4 and the delight in peace in verse 11 mark the beginning and the outcome.

In verse 5 'commit your way' is literally 'roll your way onto the LORD', the verb gol. It pictures unloading a burden onto someone able to carry it, and Proverbs 16:3 uses it, 'Commit your works to the LORD'. It is also the verb in the mockers' taunt in Psalm 22:8, 'He trusts in the LORD, let the LORD deliver him', words that the chief priests and scribes echo at the cross, Matthew 27:43. What the psalm commends as faith, the mockers throw back as an insult, and the New Testament records that Jesus did it in earnest.

The verb 'inherit' in verses 9, 11, 22, 29 and 34 is yarash, to take possession, the verb of the conquest, 'Enter and possess the land', Deuteronomy 1:8. Its counterpart is karat, 'to cut off', used in verses 9, 22, 28, 34 and 38. It is the word for cutting a covenant, and it is also used of being cut off from one's people, Genesis 17:14. The two verbs give the psalm a stark grammar: one is given a place, or is removed from it.

Finally the word acharit, 'future' or 'latter end', is at the psalm's close. 'Posterity awaits the man of peace', verse 37, and 'the future of the wicked will be cut off', verse 38. The same word marks the hope in Proverbs 23:18, 'surely there is a future'. The Bible's footnote gives the other rendering of verse 37, 'there is a future for the man of peace', and the word for peace is again shalom. The other word to notice is azab, 'forsake', in verse 25, 'abandoned', and in verse 28, 'will not forsake His saints', the root of the cry of Psalm 22:1 and of the promise, 'Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you', Hebrews 13:5.

typology.type: The inheritance of the land, verses 9, 11, 22, 29, 34
typology.fulfillment: The land promised to Abraham, Genesis 12:7, and entered by Joshua's generation is the first form of the inheritance. The New Testament widens it. Jesus says the meek will inherit 'the earth', Matthew 5:5, Paul says Abraham was to be 'heir of the world', Romans 4:13, and Peter looks for 'a new heaven and a new earth, where righteousness dwells', 2 Peter 3:13. Revelation says 'the one who overcomes will inherit all things', Revelation 21:7. The type falls short because Israel possessed the land and lost it in exile, Deuteronomy 28:63, whereas the inheritance in Christ is held by One who cannot be dislodged.

typology.type: The meek man who inherits, verse 11
typology.fulfillment: Moses is called 'a very humble man, more so than any man on the face of the earth', Numbers 12:3, and yet he was barred from the land, Numbers 20:12. Jesus is the meek one who does enter His inheritance. He calls Himself 'gentle and humble in heart', Matthew 11:29, and rides into Jerusalem as the king who comes 'gentle', Matthew 21:5, from Zechariah 9:9. He is 'appointed heir of all things', Hebrews 1:2, and His people become 'co-heirs with Christ', Romans 8:17. The type falls short in that the meekest of the old covenant could not bring his people in, and the meek of the new covenant does.

typology.type: The one who commits his way and is mocked, verse 5
typology.fulfillment: The psalm commends rolling one's way onto the LORD. The verb is thrown back at the righteous sufferer in Psalm 22:8, and the mockers at the cross say, 'He trusts in God. Let God deliver Him now if He wants Him', Matthew 27:43. Peter says that when Jesus was abused 'He did not retaliate' but 'entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly', 1 Peter 2:23. The correspondence is the pattern of trust under injustice. The escalation is that David's committing led to his rescue in this life, while Christ's led through death to resurrection, Romans 1:4.

typology.type: The steps ordered and the hand that holds, verses 23 and 24
typology.fulfillment: The man whose steps the LORD orders, and who 'though he falls, he will not be overwhelmed', is a picture of the believer, and also of Christ, who says of the Father's will, 'Your law is within my heart', Psalm 40:8, applied to Him in Hebrews 10:5-7. He is the one whose way did not falter, Psalm 37:31. He is also the one who reaches out His hand to the sinking, as with Peter on the water, Matthew 14:31. The type falls short because the psalm's righteous man does fall, while Christ never does, and it is His hand that holds.

study.christ:
The most direct line from this psalm to Jesus runs through the Beatitudes. 'Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth', Matthew 5:5, is a quotation, or nearly so, of Psalm 37:11, and Matthew's wording follows the Greek translation of the psalm closely. Jesus speaks as though it were His right to say who will inherit, and as though the promise was His to fulfil. It is also strikingly consistent with His own character. He describes Himself as 'gentle and humble in heart', Matthew 11:29, and enters Jerusalem as the king who comes gentle, Matthew 21:5. The one who pronounces the blessing is the meek man Himself.

The psalm also leads to Christ through the theme of inheritance. The Son is 'appointed heir of all things', Hebrews 1:2, and the promise of Psalm 2:8, 'I will make the nations Your inheritance, the ends of the earth Your possession', is His. What He inherits He shares. 'If you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham's seed and heirs according to the promise', Galatians 3:29, and believers are 'co-heirs with Christ', Romans 8:17. So the psalm's repeated 'will inherit the land' finds its answer in the fact that the meek who inherit do so in Him, and not by their own merit.

Third, the psalm's posture of trust is a picture of Jesus' own path. The one who commits His way to the LORD, verse 5, and waits for Him, verse 34, is what Peter describes when he says Christ 'entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly', 1 Peter 2:23. The verb that the psalm commends is thrown back by the mockers at the cross, Matthew 27:43, and He goes on trusting. The psalm's promise that the LORD will 'bring forth your righteousness like the dawn', verse 6, is answered in His resurrection, when He was 'declared with power to be the Son of God', Romans 1:4, and in the promise that 'the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father', Matthew 13:43.

There is a difficult moment that must be faced honestly. Verse 25 says, 'Never have I seen the righteous abandoned', and yet the perfectly righteous man cried out on the cross, 'My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?', Matthew 27:46. Christ was forsaken so that His people would not be. 'God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God', 2 Corinthians 5:21. The psalm's promise that the LORD 'will not forsake His saints', verse 28, holds because of that exchange. The name of the salvation in verse 39, 'The salvation of the righteous is from the LORD', is the name of Jesus, Matthew 1:21.

A caution: this is wisdom, and not a hidden prediction, and the psalm should not be turned into an allegory in which every wicked man is a figure of the devil. The wicked are ordinary people of power who oppress the poor. The psalm's first meaning matters. What the New Testament shows is that the pattern of the meek who trust and inherit has its perfect form in Christ.
study.god:
The God of Psalm 37 is not in a hurry, and the psalm wants his people to see why. He 'laughs', verse 13, and the laughter is not cruelty. It is the calm of one who sees that 'his day is coming', as the parallel in Psalm 2:4 shows, where the One enthroned in heaven laughs at the kings who plot. The wicked man's success looks large only from below. From the throne, the whole arc is visible, and the psalm invites the believer to borrow that vantage by waiting.

He is a God who knows the days of His people. 'The LORD knows the days of the blameless', verse 18, is a phrase that speaks of a knowledge that reaches every day of a person's life, the famine days as well as the plentiful ones, verse 19. It is intimate rather than distant, and it is what makes the promise that they will not be ashamed 'in the time of evil' credible.

He holds His people. In verse 23 'the steps of a man are ordered by the LORD who takes delight in his journey', and in verse 24, 'Though he falls, he will not be overwhelmed, for the LORD is holding his hand.' God is not only a rewarder at the end but a companion on the way, and His delight in the journey is remarkable. The believer's walk, with its stumbles, pleases Him. The psalm also says He 'loves justice', verse 28, and it is because He loves justice that He will not leave the righteous in the power of the wicked, verse 33.

He is a stronghold and a helper. The last verses pile up verbs: He 'helps', 'delivers', 'rescues' and 'saves', verse 40, and He is 'their stronghold in time of trouble', verse 39. It is significant that the psalm says 'in time of trouble'. God does not promise that the trouble will not come. He promises to be the fortress inside it.

The psalm holds a tension that it does not remove. God is just, but His justice waits, 'yet a little while', verse 10. The wicked flourish, verse 35, and the righteous are asked to trust that this is not the end. The Bible explains that the delay is patience and not slowness, 'not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance', 2 Peter 3:9, and that the vision 'does not lie', Habakkuk 2:3. God's patience with the wicked and His faithfulness to the righteous are both real, and only faith can hold them together.

For worship, the psalm teaches that trust is itself a form of praise. To be still before the LORD, to delight in Him, and to wait for Him honours His character more than any song of victory could, because it says, before the answer comes, that He is worth waiting for. And it reshapes desire. The believer who delights in God finds that his petitions are made new.

crossReferences.note: The Psalter's opening picture sets the righteous like a tree planted by streams against the wicked like chaff. Psalm 37 rewrites the contrast in terms of grass that withers and smoke that fades, verses 2 and 20, so that its whole argument reads as a long meditation on the two ways of the first psalm.

'The One enthroned in heaven laughs; the Lord taunts them.' Psalm 37:13 says the same of the wicked who plot against the righteous, 'the Lord laughs, seeing that their day is coming'. The laugh in both places is the composure of a king who knows how the conspiracy ends.

An earlier psalm promises that the one who fears the LORD will have a soul that dwells in prosperity and 'his descendants will inherit the land'. Psalm 37 takes the promise and repeats it as a refrain, and shows that the inheritance is meant to be long term.

'Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it.' The same first two commands open Psalm 37:27. The two psalms, both acrostics, teach the same way of life, and both end by saying the LORD saves those who take refuge in Him, Psalm 34:22 and Psalm 37:40.

The psalmist who envied the wicked's prosperity finds the answer only when he enters God's sanctuary and discerns their end. Psalm 37 gives the same answer by observation and waiting, and the two psalms show two roads to the same confidence, that the end is not what it looks like now.

'Do not fret over evildoers, and do not be envious of the wicked.' It repeats Psalm 37:1 almost word for word. The link shows that the psalm is a piece of Israel's shared wisdom, and that its first command was a proverb before it was a psalm.

The prophet asks, 'Why does the way of the wicked prosper?' It is the question Psalm 37 addresses. Jeremiah puts it as a complaint and is told to expect harder things, so the two texts together show that faith may ask the question, and that the answer requires patience.

'Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth.' Jesus quotes Psalm 37:11 and reads the promise in its widest sense. The Bible's own footnote at the psalm notes that the Hebrew can mean the earth as well as the land, so the reading was open from the start.

Paul says the promise to Abraham was that he would be 'heir of the world', and that it came through faith and not law. It shows the apostle reading the land promise, which Psalm 37 repeats, as a promise about the whole creation that would be given through the righteousness of faith.

The patriarchs died without receiving what was promised, seeing it from afar, and they were 'longing for a better country, a heavenly one'. It is the New Testament's explanation of why the psalm's land promise must be read beyond the borders of Canaan.

Christ, abused, did not retaliate but 'entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly'. It is the fullest example of the psalm's way of committing one's cause to the LORD, and it is offered by Peter as a pattern for suffering Christians.

'My God, My God, why have You forsaken me?' The verb behind 'forsaken' is the one in Psalm 37:25 and 28. The cry of the righteous sufferer in Psalm 22 stands against the psalm's claim that the righteous are not abandoned, and the cross shows how both are true.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a gift of the earth. God told the first human beings to 'fill the earth and subdue it', Genesis 1:28, and the psalmist later says, 'the earth He has given to mankind', Psalm 115:16. The story of the fall is a story of losing that inheritance, when the man was banished from the garden and cherubim were stationed on the east, Genesis 3:23-24. Ever since, the world has been held, it seems, by the wrong people. Psalm 37 is a song for people who live in that world, where the proud are prosperous and the faithful are pressed, and who are told that this is not the end.

The promise of land is the thread by which the psalm is tied to the rest of the story. God told Abram, 'I will give this land to your offspring', Genesis 12:7, and Israel entered it under Joshua. But Israel was warned that they could be uprooted, Deuteronomy 28:63, and they were. The psalm's promise to the meek was sung by people who had known both possession and loss, and it kept alive the idea that the land is finally given to those who trust the LORD, and not to those who grab it. The prophets keep the hope alive: 'they will possess the land forever', Isaiah 60:21.

Jesus is the turning point. He is the meek man who is appointed heir of all things, Hebrews 1:2, and He speaks the psalm's promise over His disciples, Matthew 5:5. In Him the inheritance is enlarged from a strip of land to the world, Romans 4:13, and it is given to all who belong to Him, Galatians 3:29. He also lives the psalm's pattern. He commits Himself to the Father under injustice, 1 Peter 2:23, is forsaken for the sake of those who trust Him, Matthew 27:46, and is raised, Romans 1:4.

The story ends with the promise kept. 'The one who overcomes will inherit all things', Revelation 21:7, and there is a new heaven and a new earth where righteousness dwells, 2 Peter 3:13. The psalm's picture of the wicked who are 'no more', though you look for them, verse 10, has its echo in the great white throne from which earth and heaven flee and 'no place was found for them', Revelation 20:11. And 'God will wipe away every tear from their eyes', Revelation 21:4. The waiting is over, the fretting is done, and the meek have the earth.

sermon.title: Battling the Unbelief of Envy
sermon.why: Piper preaches directly on Psalm 37:1-7, showing that envy of the wicked's prosperity is at root a failure to believe God's promises, and that trusting, delighting in, and committing our way to the LORD is the biblical answer to that unbelief.

quiz.q: What does the psalm say happens to those who do evil, despite their apparent success?

options.text: They wither quickly like grass and will soon be no more, though they seem to flourish now.
options.note: Verses 2, 10, and 20 all describe the wicked's prosperity as brief, like grass, smoke, or the glory of the fields.

options.text: They will prosper forever without any consequence.
options.note: The psalm consistently teaches the opposite, their prosperity is temporary.

options.text: They will be given the land as their permanent inheritance.
options.note: The land inheritance is promised to the meek and righteous, not the wicked, who will be cut off.

options.text: They will eventually repent and be restored.
options.note: The psalm speaks of the wicked being cut off and vanishing, not of their repentance and restoration.

quiz.q: According to verse 11, who will inherit the land and delight in abundant prosperity?

options.text: The meek, the anavim, those who are humble and dependent on God.
options.note: This is the exact promise Jesus repeats in Matthew 5:5, 'Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth.'

options.text: The wealthy and powerful.
options.note: The psalm contrasts the meek with the wicked, not with the poor; wealth and power are not the criterion.

options.text: Only the priests and Levites.
options.note: The psalm addresses the righteous and meek in general, not a particular tribe or office.

options.text: Those who take vengeance on their enemies.
options.note: The psalm actually counsels refraining from anger and wrath, verse 8, not taking vengeance.

quiz.q: What lifelong testimony does the psalmist give in verse 25?

options.text: He has never seen the righteous abandoned or their children begging for bread.
options.note: This is the psalmist's personal, long-observed testimony to God's faithful care for the righteous.

options.text: He has seen many righteous people suffer complete ruin.
options.note: The testimony given is the opposite, a witness to the LORD's sustaining care over a lifetime.

options.text: He has never met a righteous person.
options.note: The testimony assumes the psalmist has observed many righteous people over a long life.

options.text: He expects to see the righteous suffer in his old age.
options.note: The testimony is retrospective confidence based on a lifetime of observation, not a future expectation of suffering.

quiz.q: How does Jesus directly connect Himself to this psalm's central promise?

options.text: He repeats its exact promise in Matthew 5:5, 'Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth.'
options.note: Jesus takes the psalm's promise to the meek and widens it into a beatitude of His kingdom.

options.text: He never references this psalm anywhere in His teaching.
options.note: Jesus explicitly quotes this psalm's promise in the Beatitudes.

options.text: He reverses the promise, saying the proud will inherit the earth.
options.note: Jesus affirms rather than reverses the psalm's promise to the meek.

options.text: He applies the promise only to Israel's physical land, not any wider inheritance.
options.note: Jesus widens the promise from the land to the whole earth, not narrowing it.

quiz.q: What is the psalm's counsel for facing the wicked's apparent prosperity?

options.text: Do not fret or envy them, but trust, delight in, and wait patiently for the LORD.
options.note: This is the psalm's repeated refrain, given in verses 1, 3-5, 7-8, and 34.

options.text: Imitate their methods to gain similar success.
options.note: The psalm explicitly warns against envying or imitating the wicked, not adopting their ways.

options.text: Confront them publicly and demand justice immediately.
options.note: The psalm counsels stillness and patient trust in the LORD's timing, not immediate public confrontation.

options.text: Accept that God is indifferent to the outcome.
options.note: The psalm insists God sees, laughs at the wicked's schemes, and will certainly act, not that He is indifferent.

questions: The psalm opens by naming envy and fretting over the wicked as a real temptation. Where in your life are you tempted to envy someone whose prosperity seems to come from wrongdoing, and what would it look like to trust instead?

David says, 'Delight yourself in the LORD, and He will give you the desires of your heart.' How does delighting in God, rather than merely using Him to get what you want, actually reshape what your heart desires?

The psalm commends qavah, taut, expectant waiting, twice. What are you currently waiting for God to do, and how might expectant hope look different from either giving up or taking matters into your own hands?

David's testimony in verse 25 rests on a long life of observation. What have you personally observed, over years, about God's faithfulness to those who trust Him, even if the timing was not what you expected?

Jesus takes up this psalm's promise to the meek directly in the Beatitudes. How does knowing that Jesus Himself embodied perfect meekness and trust change the way you read David's counsel to commit your way to the LORD?

translationNotes.note: Fret renders a Hebrew root, charah, meaning to become heated or to kindle anger, picturing an inward burning agitation rather than mere worry.
Hope renders qavah, a word rooted in the image of a taut, stretched cord, describing expectant, straining hope rather than passive resignation.
Meek renders anavim, describing humility and dependence on God rather than mere gentleness of temperament; this is the exact word and promise Jesus repeats in Matthew 5:5.
